facts.text: The only hitter of the 1960s to collect 180 hits and score 65 runs or fewer: Matty Alou, 1968 — 185 H, 59 R.
The only hitter of the 1960s to drive in 150 runs: Tommy Davis, 1962 — 153 RBI.
The only pitcher of the 1960s to strike out 200 and win 9 games or fewer: Sam McDowell, 1966 — 225 K, 9-8.
The only pitcher of the 1960s to strike out 300 without winning 20: Sam McDowell, 1965 — 325 K, 17-11.
The only hitter of the 1960s to score 120 runs with 50 RBI or fewer: Maury Wills, 1962 — 130 R, 48 RBI.
The only hitter of the 1960s to bat .320 at age 37 or older (500+ PA): Stan Musial, 1962 — .330 at 41.
The only hitter of the 1960s to hit 30+ homers at age 37 or older: Ernie Banks, 1968 — 32 HR at 37.
Only two hitters of the 1960s collected 230 hits: Matty Alou (1969, 231 H); Tommy Davis (1962, 230 H).
The only hitter of the 1960s to drive in 100 runs with an OPS under .700: Joe Pepitone, 1964 — 100 RBI, .699 OPS.
The only hitter of the 1960s to bat .330 at age 22 or younger (500+ PA): Vada Pinson, 1961 — .343 at 22.
The only pitcher of the 1960s to post an ERA under 3.00 and win 7 or fewer (162+ IP): Don Cardwell, 1968 — 2.96 ERA, 7-13.
The only hitter of the 1960s to hit 30+ homers while batting under .230 (400+ PA): Ken Harrelson, 1969 — 30 HR, .221.
The only hitter of the 1960s to bat .310 while slugging under .380 (500+ PA): Curt Flood, 1964 — .311 AVG, .378 SLG.
Only two hitters of the 1960s went 30-30: Bobby Bonds (1969, 32 HR, 45 SB); Hank Aaron (1963, 44 HR, 31 SB).
Just three hitters of the 1960s drew 100 walks and struck out 140 times: Jimmy Wynn (1969, 148 BB, 142 K); Reggie Jackson (1969, 114 BB, 142 K); Harmon Killebrew (1962, 106 BB, 142 K).
Willie Mays drove in 100+ runs in 7 straight seasons (1960-66), the longest run of the 1960s.
Roberto Clemente batted .300 or better (500+ PA) in 8 straight seasons (1960-67), the longest run of the 1960s.
Only two hitters of the 1960s hit 35+ homers with 15 doubles or fewer: Harmon Killebrew (1964, 49 HR, 11 2B); Jim Lemon (1960, 38 HR, 10 2B).
Only two hitters of the 1960s stole 40+ bases with an on-base under .300 (400+ PA): Bert Campaneris (1967, 55 SB, .297 OBP); Luis Aparicio (1963, 40 SB, .291 OBP).
Just four hitters of the 1960s stole 70 bases: Maury Wills (1962, 104 SB); Maury Wills (1965, 94 SB); Lou Brock (1966, 74 SB); Tommy Harper (1969, 73 SB).
Willie Mays hit 30+ home runs in 6 straight seasons (1961-66), the longest run of the 1960s.
Lou Brock stole 40+ bases in 6 straight seasons (1964-69), the longest run of the 1960s.
Sandy Koufax struck out 200+ in 6 straight seasons (1961-66), the longest run of the 1960s.
Don Drysdale threw 250+ innings in 6 straight seasons (1962-67), the longest run of the 1960s.

Just three hitters of the 1960s batted .300 with 30 homers, 100 RBI and 20 steals: Hank Aaron (1963, .319, 44 HR, 130 RBI, 31 SB); Frank Robinson (1961, .323, 37 HR, 124 RBI, 22 SB); Hank Aaron (1961, .327, 34 HR, 120 RBI, 21 SB).

Just four pitchers of the 1960s won 15+ games at age 38 or older: Warren Spahn (1963, 23-7 at 42); Warren Spahn (1961, 21-13 at 40); Warren Spahn (1960, 21-10 at 39); Warren Spahn (1962, 18-14 at 41).
Just three hitters of the 1960s posted a .400 on-base with 5 homers or fewer (500+ PA): Richie Ashburn (1960, .415 OBP, 0 HR); Pete Runnels (1960, .401 OBP, 2 HR); Joe Morgan (1966, .410 OBP, 5 HR).
Just three pitchers of the 1960s won 20 and lost 15 in the same season: Fergie Jenkins (1969, 21-15); Fergie Jenkins (1968, 20-15); Claude Osteen (1969, 20-15).
Just three hitters of the 1960s grounded into 28+ double plays: Carl Yastrzemski (1964, 30 GIDP); Brooks Robinson (1960, 29 GIDP); Frank Howard (1969, 29 GIDP).
Just three hitters of the 1960s hit 30+ homers at age 22 or younger: Boog Powell (1964, 39 HR at 22); Tony Conigliaro (1965, 32 HR at 20); Jim Ray Hart (1964, 31 HR at 22).
Just three hitters of the 1960s drew more walks than hits (400+ PA): Jimmy Wynn (1969, 148 BB, 133 H); Mickey Mantle (1968, 106 BB, 103 H); Mickey Mantle (1962, 122 BB, 121 H).
25 times in the 1960s a pitcher threw 300 innings. The most extreme: Denny McLain, 1968 — 336.0 IP.

Just four pitchers of the 1960s won 18+ games at age 22 or younger: Wally Bunker (1964, 19-5 at 19); Denny McLain (1966, 20-14 at 22); Larry Dierker (1969, 20-13 at 22); Chuck Estrada (1960, 18-11 at 22).
Most strikeouts by a .300 hitter of the 1960s: Dick Allen, 1965 — 150 K while batting .302.
Most steals by a 30-homer hitter of the 1960s: Bobby Bonds, 1969 — 45 SB with 32 HR.
Fewest strikeouts by a 30-homer hitter of the 1960s: Felix Mantilla, 1964 — 46 K with 30 HR.
Most walks by a sub-.240 hitter of the 1960s: Joe Morgan, 1969 — 110 BB while batting .236.
Most RBI per home run among 100-RBI seasons: Floyd Robinson, 1962 — 109 RBI on 11 HR.
Most wins by a pitcher with an ERA over 5.00: Phil Ortega, 1965 — 12-15 with a 5.11 ERA.
Fewest wins by a qualified pitcher with an ERA under 3.00: Don Cardwell, 1968 — 7-13 despite a 2.96 ERA.
Most losses by a pitcher with an ERA under 3.50: Turk Farrell, 1962 — 10-20 with a 3.02 ERA.
Fewest strikeouts by a 20-game winner of the 1960s: Dick Donovan, 1962 — 94 K, 20-10.
Most innings in a season without a complete game: Eddie Fisher, 1965 — 165.1 IP, 0 CG.
Most walks by a 15-game winner: Chuck Estrada, 1961 — 132 BB, 15-9.
21 hitter-seasons of the 1960s ended on exactly 29 home runs, one short of 30 — among them Billy Williams (1966), Dick Allen (1964), Roberto Clemente (1966).
22 pitcher-seasons of the 1960s ended on exactly 19 wins, one short of 20 — among them Gaylord Perry (1969), Don Drysdale (1963), Jim Bunning (1966).
Juan Marichal won 20 games in 4 straight seasons (1963-66), the longest run of the 1960s.
10 teams of the 1960s won 100 games; the best record was the 1961 Yankees at 109-53.
Youngest player of the 1960s to hit 30 home runs: Tony Conigliaro, age 20 in 1965 — 32 HR.
Oldest player of the 1960s to hit 30 home runs: Ernie Banks, age 37 in 1968 — 32 HR.
Youngest player of the 1960s to bat .330 (500+ PA): Vada Pinson, age 22 in 1961 — .343.
Oldest player of the 1960s to bat .330 (500+ PA): Stan Musial, age 41 in 1962 — .330.
Youngest player of the 1960s to drive in 100 runs: Willie Horton, age 22 in 1965 — 104 RBI.
Youngest player of the 1960s to steal 40 bases: Sonny Jackson, age 21 in 1966 — 49 SB.
Youngest player of the 1960s to strike out 200: Gary Nolan, age 19 in 1967 — 206 K.
Oldest player of the 1960s to strike out 200: Jim Bunning, age 35 in 1967 — 253 K.
Youngest player of the 1960s to post a qualified ERA under 2.75: Wally Bunker, age 19 in 1964 — 2.69 ERA.
2 teams of the 1960s had three players at 100+ RBI; the biggest pairing was the 1966 Baltimore Orioles — Frank Robinson 122, Boog Powell 109, Brooks Robinson 100.
4 teams of the 1960s had two players at 200+ hits; the biggest pairing was the 1963 St. Louis Cardinals — Dick Groat 201, Bill White 200, Curt Flood 200.
16 teams of the 1960s had two players at 200+ strikeouts; the biggest pairing was the 1969 Houston Astros — Don Wilson 235, Larry Dierker 232, Tom Griffin 200.
Most strikeouts by a hitter in the 1960s: Frank Howard, 1103.
Most wins of the 1960s: Juan Marichal, 191.
Most losses of the 1960s: Jack Fisher, 133 — and 85 wins.
Most strikeouts of the 1960s: Bob Gibson, 2071.
Most saves of the 1960s: Hoyt Wilhelm, 152.
Most walks issued in the 1960s: Steve Barber, 834.
1969 had 17 30-homer hitters, the most of any season in the 1960s.
1968 had just 7 30-homer hitters, the fewest of any season in the 1960s.
1962 had 23 .300 hitters (500+ PA), the most of any season in the 1960s.
1968 had just 6 .300 hitters (500+ PA), the fewest of any season in the 1960s.
1962 had 18 100-RBI hitters, the most of any season in the 1960s.
1968 had just 3 100-RBI hitters, the fewest of any season in the 1960s.
1969 had 8 40-steal players, the most of any season in the 1960s.
1961 had just 1 40-steal players, the fewest of any season in the 1960s.
1964 had 6 200-hit seasons, the most of any season in the 1960s.
1960 had no 200-hit seasons at all — the only season of the 1960s without one.
1969 had 15 20-game winners, the most of any season in the 1960s.
1960 had just 3 20-game winners, the fewest of any season in the 1960s.
18 teams of the 1960s lost 100 games; the worst was the 1962 Mets at 40-120.
Best run differential of the 1960s: the 1969 Orioles, +262 (779 scored, 517 allowed).
5 times in the 1960s a pitcher allowed 35+ homers and still won 15. The most extreme: Ralph Terry, 1962 — 40 HR allowed, 23-12.
2 hitter-seasons of the 1960s ended on exactly 199 hits, one short of 200 — among them Dick Groat (1962), Bill White (1962).
Worst run differential of the 1960s: the 1962 Mets, -331 (617 scored, 948 allowed).
11 times in the 1960s a hitter got hit by 15+ pitches. The most extreme: Ron Hunt, 1968 — 25 HBP.
16 times in the 1960s a pitcher lost 20 games. The most extreme: Roger Craig, 1962 — 10-24.
17 times in the 1960s a pitcher won 12+ games without a start. The most extreme: Ron Perranoski, 1963 — 16-3, 0 GS.
12 times in the 1960s a pitcher threw 8+ shutouts. The most extreme: Bob Gibson, 1968 — 13 SHO.
10 times in the 1960s a hitter struck out 25 times or fewer in a full season (600+ PA). The most extreme: Nellie Fox, 1961 — 12 K in 696 PA.
13 times in the 1960s a hitter hit 12+ triples and more triples than homers. The most extreme: Tony Gonzalez, 1963 — 12 3B, 4 HR.
30 times in the 1960s a pitcher posted a WHIP of 1.00 or lower (162+ IP). The most extreme: Dave McNally, 1968 — 0.84 WHIP in 273.0 IP.
6 times in the 1960s a pitcher posted an ERA under 2.50 with a losing record (25+ starts). The most extreme: Joe Horlen, 1966 — 2.43 ERA, 10-13.

method: Every fact is a predicate evaluated over every hitter-season and pitcher-season in the decade, pulled in full from the MLB Stats API (the official record). Nothing is recalled or estimated; the rows that satisfy each rule are stored with it.

'Only', 'two' and 'three/four' claims are exact counts across the complete pull. Where a rule uses a plate-appearance or innings floor instead of a league qualification bar, the floor is stated in the fact so the claim is reproducible.
Thresholds are era-aware (strikeouts, saves and home runs meant different things in 1925 and 1995) and are recorded in the file.
Rules built from plain comparisons carry a Stathead Season Finder spec with the same filters and year range, for independent re-checking on the subscription.
